n69-pem.title: Blind feedlot lamb: gray versus white matter

text.title: Blind feedlot lamb: gray versus white matter
text.history: After a rapid shift to a high-concentrate ration, a lamb becomes dull, develops cortical blindness and head-pressing, and then has seizures. No obvious ocular abnormality explains the blindness. The cerebral cortex is subtly swollen and yellow-gray; some gyri are flattened.
text.gross: Bilaterally distributed cortical swelling, yellow discoloration and softening; chronic lesions may become cavitated. A Wood's lamp may demonstrate cortical autofluorescence, but absence does not exclude the disease.
text.histo: Laminar neuronal necrosis in the cerebral gray matter, with neuronal eosinophilia and nuclear pyknosis, neuropil vacuolation, edema and variable macrophage reaction depending on duration.
text.morph: Cerebrum: bilateral, laminar, cortical neuronal necrosis (polioencephalomalacia)
text.mechanism: Polioencephalomalacia describes the cortical lesion pattern, not one uniquely identified agent. In ruminants it can follow disruption of thiamine availability/metabolism or high sulfur exposure. Energy failure preferentially injures metabolically active cortical neurons.
text.tests: Assess diet, ration transition, sulfur in water/feed and possible thiamine-related risk factors; evaluate response to treatment clinically. Histology establishes the lesion pattern but cannot distinguish sulfur-associated from thiamine-associated injury alone.

text.title: Horse with acute cerebral malacia
text.history: A horse that has eaten contaminated moldy corn develops abrupt blindness, head pressing and seizures. On sectioning the brain, cerebral white matter is softened and liquefied while much of the gray matter is relatively spared.
text.gross: Pale/yellow softened or cavitated regions concentrated in cerebral white matter.
text.histo: Liquefactive necrosis and degeneration of white matter, with macrophages during lesion evolution.
text.morph: Cerebrum: multifocal to regionally extensive leukoencephalomalacia
text.mechanism: Fusarium-associated fumonisin B1 toxicosis causes preferential severe injury to equine cerebral white matter. The professor notes its tissue selectivity is incompletely explained.
text.tests: Feed/exposure history and toxin testing support the association; evaluate the lesion distribution and exclude other toxic/vascular causes.

text.title: Published case · Boxer with persistent alopecia and abdominal mass
text.species: 6-year-old male Boxer; unilateral orchiectomy at six months, with a contralateral retained testis
text.reproductiveStatus: Unilaterally castrated at six months; contralateral testis retained (cryptorchid)
text.history: A 6-year-old Boxer underwent removal of one testis at six months of age. Approximately 18 months later he developed persistent generalized alopecia and pruritus and was treated for presumed atopic dermatitis for years without resolution of the alopecia. Clinical signs: Bilateral alopecia, moderate-to-severe scale and lichenification of the sternum, axillae and medial thighs; lichenified and edematous scrotal skin; pendulous, edematous prepuce; elongated/enlarged mammary papillae. Ancillary diagnostics: CBC and serum chemistry were within reported normal limits. Preputial cytology contained superficial epithelial cells. Abdominal ultrasound showed a 4.2 × 3.3 cm irregular, heterogeneous, moderately cystic mass just cranioventral and left of the urinary bladder, suspicious for retained testicular tissue. Mild–moderate iliac lymph node enlargement and splenic nodules were noted; their aspirates supported reactive/hyperplastic changes rather than proven metastasis. Thoracic radiographs showed no pulmonary metastases.
text.gross: Following exploratory laparotomy, a retained left abdominal testis adjacent to the urinary bladder was removed. It measured 5.0 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm and was multinodular, irregularly contoured and partly replaced by a soft tan multinodular mass with multiple brown-fluid-filled cysts.
text.histo: The left testis contained a partially encapsulated, infiltrative, multilobular sex-cord stromal neoplasm. Polygonal-to-elongated neoplastic cells formed coalescing lobules divided by fibrous trabeculae and palisaded along connective-tissue bands. Residual seminiferous tubules were markedly atrophic, devoid of germ cells. Tumor emboli occurred in testicular and pampiniform-plexus vessels; the sampled medial iliac node contained no neoplastic cells.
text.morph: Left abdominal testis: expansile, multilobular, partially infiltrative neoplasm with cystic change, marked adjacent tubular atrophy, and histologically confirmed vascular invasion.
text.mechanism: Neoplastic Sertoli cells can produce endocrine signals including anti-Müllerian hormone and inhibin; tumor-associated estrogenic activity altered hair follicle cycling and contributed to bilateral alopecia and feminization (pendulous prepuce and enlarged mammary papillae). The concurrent pruritus may have reflected separate allergic skin disease. The steep declines in AMH and inhibin B following removal support a gonadal tumor source, but hormone concentrations alone do not establish the microscopic tumor type. Vascular tumor emboli raised future metastatic-risk concerns despite negative staging tests at presentation.
text.tests: Article-confirmed investigations: preputial cytology (superficial epithelial cells); ultrasonography localizing a heterogeneous 4.2 × 3.3 cm retained abdominal testis; normal CBC and serum chemistry; splenic and iliac node cytology; thoracic radiographs without pulmonary metastases; surgical removal with testis, spermatic cord and lymph-node histopathology. AMH decreased from 8,435 to 56 ng/mL three weeks after surgery (reported adult male intact interval 0.2–73.4 ng/mL; castrated interval <0.15 ng/mL, assay-specific). Inhibin B decreased from about 807 to <6 pg/mL; the article reports no comparable reference interval. Estrone sulphate was 1.5 before and 1.3 ng/mL after surgery, without an established canine male reference interval. Recheck and surveillance were advised because of vascular invasion.

options.name: Sertoli cell tumor (cryptorchid retained testis)
options.supports: Absent contralateral scrotal testis, suspicious abdominal gonadal mass, bilateral alopecia and feminization changes; tumor histology ultimately confirms Sertoli cell differentiation.
options.against: Endocrine signs and ultrasonography alone cannot prove Sertoli cell tumor; other testicular tumors must be distinguished microscopically.
options.hist: Palisading polygonal-to-elongated neoplastic cells in multilobular fibrous stroma, with seminiferous tubular atrophy and vascular emboli.

options.name: Seminoma in a retained testis
options.supports: Cryptorchid testes are predisposed to neoplasia; seminoma can present as an abdominal testicular mass.
options.against: Feminization and hormonal manifestations favor Sertoli cell tumor. Seminoma usually shows sheets of germ cells rather than the described Sertoli-type palisading architecture.
options.hist: Large round germ-cell populations in sheets, sometimes with lymphocytic infiltrates, rather than sex-cord tubular/palisading arrangement.

options.name: Leydig (interstitial) cell tumor
options.supports: Older male dogs may develop endocrine-associated testicular tumors and interstitial tumors can alter hormonal profiles.
options.against: Often small, soft, yellow-orange or brown testicular nodules rather than this invasive, cystic retained-testis mass; Sertoli cell tumor better explains the full presentation.
options.hist: Nests or sheets of interstitial endocrine cells without the characteristic Sertoli-cell palisading and fibrous trabecular pattern.

options.name: Chronic allergic dermatitis / atopic dermatitis as sole explanation
options.supports: Pruritus and scaling were genuine concerns and some residual itch responded to anti-IL-31 therapy.
options.against: Does not explain the absent testis, abdominal gonadal mass, enlarged mammary papillae, pendulous prepuce and endocrine-marker decline after tumor removal. Separate allergic disease could coexist.
options.hist: Inflammatory skin changes cannot account for the testicular sex-cord stromal neoplasm; the removed testis reveals the decisive pathology.

text.gross: Diffuse flattening of gyri and narrowed sulci; brain may herniate
text.dx: Brain: diffuse edema
text.histo: Vasogenic: extracellular white matter fluid; cytotoxic: swollen cells
text.why: BBB disruption or ATP-dependent pump failure
text.notes:
Two types: Cytotoxic edema and vasogenic

Cytotoxic edema:
Accumulation of fluid intracellularly in astrocytes, endothelial cells, neurons, and
oligodendrocytes
• Secondary to altered cellular metabolism
• Interference with Na+/K+-ATPase pump
• Can’t maintain cellular homeostasis
• Results in elevated intracellular sodium and thus influx of water
• Blood-brain barrier remains intact
• Causes of cytotoxic edema:
• Hypoxia-ischemia
• Severe hypothermia
• Some toxicants

Vasogenic edema:
Most common type of edema in the CNS
• Occurs after vascular injury adjacent to inflammation, hematomas, contusions,
infarcts, cerebral hypertension, or neoplasms
• An increase in vascular permeability from the breakdown of the blood-brain barrier
• Allows movement of plasma constituents (water, ions, plasma proteins) into the extracellular
space
• Can be accompanied by some cellular
 swelling involving astrocytes
• Increases intracranial pressure
• If severe, pressure can cause neurologic
 dysfunction and caudal displacement of
 brain structures
(ie. coning of the cerebellar vermis)

pathx-68-9.title: Overeating disease — C. perfringens type D

text.gross: Gross: Often no visible lesion. When present, bilateral symmetric yellow/gray/red foci of malacia and cavitation preferentially in white matter. Do not confuse: Symmetric toxin-associated white matter lesions versus random septic embolic lesions from TME.
text.dx: **Working identification: **Overeating disease — ***C. perfringens type D.*** Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why:
**Species and trigger:** Sheep and goats of any age after sudden* diet* change causing microbial imbalance and clostridial proliferation. 
**Why CNS damage occurs: **Enterotoxemia produces vascular injury and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier.

text.gross: Often no gross visible mass; when present, irregular gray-white to red, gelatinous/granular foci in white matter, especially brainstem. Can have a gelatinous or granular consistency.
text.dx:
Working identification: Granulomatous meningoencephalitis (GME). 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges. 
Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity, and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.

text.why:
**Idiopathic condition. **

 Differentiate: GME perivascular inflammation from the suppurative microabscesses of Listeria or thrombotic lesions of Histophilus.
text.notes:
Most severe in the brainstem (white matter) 
**Clinical:** Behavior change, circling, seizures; paresis and ataxia when spinal cord is involved. 

**Differentiate:** GME perivascular inflammation from the suppurative microabscesses of Listeria or thrombotic lesions of *Histophilus.*

Blood flow failure causes energy depletion and necrosis; distribution follows vessel.
More rapid ischemia → more severe lesion
• Sudden obstruction (ex: embolus, compression) → neurons die
within minutes

Granular, gray-white plexus with hyperemia/hemorrhage and cloudy to yellow-green, thick or gelatinous in the ventricular system.

text.dx: Working identification: Choroid plexitis. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Location: Inflammation of the choroid plexus, most commonly due to bacteria entering directly or hematogenously, though viral infection is possible. Why it matters: Inflammation may extend through CSF spaces into the leptomeninges, and purulent exudate can impede CSF flow, causing acquired hydrocephalus.
text.why: Why it matters: Inflammation may extend through CSF spaces into leptomeninges, and purulent exudate can impede CSF flow, causing acquired hydrocephalus. Differentiate: Choroid plexus is the CSF-producing structure; ependyma lines the ventricular wall.
text.notes:
If severe, it can traverse the fourth ventricle and spread throughout the subarachnoid space, causing suppurative leptomeningitis. The exudate can also obstruct the CSF flow *which can lead to hydrocephalus. *

Also called Ependymitis.

text.gross: Opaque, hyperemic meninges (typically referring to leptomeninges) with yellow-white exudate tracking sulci; distinguish inflammation of pia/arachnoid and subarachnoid space from thickened inflamed dura.
text.dx: CNS meninges: diffuse fibrinosuppurative leptomeningitis (working pattern; etiology pending)
text.histo: Suppurative leptomeningitis: abundant neutrophils/fibrin within the subarachnoid space. Nonsuppurative: lymphocytes/mononuclear cells. Granulomatous: macrophages/giant cells and possible fungi. Pachymeningitis: dura. Meningoencephalitis: adjacent brain parenchyma.
text.why:
Septicemia or contiguous infection can seed the meninges; gross appearance and leukocyte pattern localize and classify inflammation, but bacterial identity requires laboratory confirmation. Can be spread by direct extension or leukocyte trafficking. 
Most commonly caused by bacteria that reach the leptomeninges and subarachnoid space** hematogenously. **
text.notes:
Strict viral leptomeningitis is rare (those tend to cause meningoencephalitis)
Can have multiple levels of chronicitiy.

pathx-68-25.title: Fungal CNS infections — overview and differential etiologies

text.gross: Moderately well demarcated, expansive, yellow- brown foci that displace and disrupt normal tissue.
text.dx:
Most cases are opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals. 
Aspergillus is an example of trophism for vessels (angioinvasive) and can cause vasculitis leading to thrombosis or infarction. 

**Working identification:** Fungal CNS infections — overview and differential etiologies. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges.
text.histo:
Granulomatous to pyogranulomatous inflammation with spores able to be seen in samples. 
Can have angioinvasive with vessel trophism species.
text.why: **Fungal agents in professor's list:** *Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus neoformans, the historical 'Zygomycetes' group, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma capsulatum and Coccidioides spp. *

text.gross: Cloudy/viscous leptomeninges and multiple small cyst-like lesions with a viscous, *gelatinous* appearance of the meninges or CNS parenchyma.
text.dx:
Working identification:* Cryptococcosis — C. neoformans / C. gattii*. 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
*Cryptococcus spp. secrete a thick complex polysaccharide capsule that protects the fungus from host defenses*
text.histo: Encapsulated budding yeasts, often with a prominent clear halo around the organism; inflammation varies with host immune response. Confirm with microbiology.
text.why: Hosts: Particular CNS affinity in cats and dogs, occasionally horses.
text.notes:
**Diagnostic confirmation:** Evaluate tissue cytology/histology and organism identification; fungal antigen testing can support cryptococcosis. A gross lesion alone does not prove etiology.
**Route of infection:**
• Enters the leptomeninges by direct extension through the
cribriform plate after a nasal or sinus infection
• Hematogenous usually from a pulmonary infection.
• Spread of the infection can result in encephalitis and ventriculitis

Immunosuppression (i.e viral infections or long term
glucocorticoid) can increase susceptibility
• Immunocompetent animals usually clear the infection before it spreads systemically

text.gross:
Hemorrhage or necrosis; *multifocal necrosis with glial nodules and mixed inflammation*; yellow-brown-gray granular foci in gray or white matter. 
**Chronic: **Larger granular discolored areas may blur gray-white boundaries.
text.dx:
Working identification: Neosporosis — Neospora caninum. Affinity for the nervous system. 
**Transmission:** Ingestion of cysts or transplacental infection 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord/meninges. 
Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Can see oocysts, tachyzoites, or bradyzoites, depending on the stage, which aids in chronicity.
text.why:
**Host and transmission:** Dogs, cattle and other mammals; infection can follow ingestion of cysts or transplacental spread. 
**Age differences**: Young dogs: polyradiculoneuritis/polymyositis; adult dogs: encephalitis (often cerebellum) and myositis.
text.notes:
Neurologic disease can be divided into two categories:
- Polyradiculoneuritis and polymyositis: young dogs
-Encephalitis (predilection for cerebellum_ and myosititis: adult dogs 
**Stages**
Oocysts (environmental stages formed in canine intestinal epithelium and passed with the feces)
Tachyzoites (asexual rapidly growing stages that actively invade tissues; present during acute phase of infection.

Bradyzoites (slowly dividing stages that encyst within tissues)

text.gross: No consistent gray-versus-white-matter predilection in the CNS. Focal hemorrhage and necrosis may develop into yellow-brown to gray, granular foci; spinal nerve roots may also be involved.
text.dx: Working identification: Toxoplasmosis due to Toxoplasma gondii. Specimen site: brain / spinal cord / meninges. For a morphologic diagnosis, specify the observed tissue and inflammation/necrosis pattern, distribution, and supported severity; the gross appearance alone cannot establish etiology.
text.histo: Protozoal infection can involve neurons and astrocytes with necrosis and associated hemorrhage/inflammation. The pattern and identification of organisms require histologic confirmation.
text.why: Toxoplasma gondii is an obligate intracellular protozoan. Transplacental infection can affect the developing CNS. In mature animals, clinically apparent CNS disease may occur with immunosuppression, including concurrent canine distemper. Differentiate this protozoal disease from nematode larval migration by organism and lesion pattern.
text.notes:
This parasite targets different cell types. Parasitizes variety of cell types (lungs, lymphoid system, liver, heart, skeletal muscle, pancreas,
gastrointestinal (GI) tract, eyes, and nervous system)
• CNS infection targets neurons and astrocytes

In mature animals, T. gondii infections have been associated with immunosuppression, like canine distempter virus.

text.why: Mechanism: Fibrocartilage from intervertebral disk reaches spinal cord vasculature, causing occlusive emboli and acute ischemia. Host: Most commonly dogs, especially larger breeds, though reported across domestic species.
text.etiologyAgents:
Ischemic myelopathy
Fibrocartilaginous embolic myelopathy, FCE

text.gross: Severe complication: Myelomalacia can spread cranially and caudally with gray/white matter necrosis and hemorrhage, sometimes within 12–24 hours.
text.dx: Working identification: Intervertebral disk disease (IVDD). Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Mechanism: Direct spinal compression injures axons (Wallerian degeneration) and may impair blood supply, causing ischemia and malacia. Severe complication: Myelomalacia can spread cranially and caudally with gray/white matter necrosis and hemorrhage, sometimes within 12–24 hours.
text.why:
Especially common in chondrodystrophic dogs.
 **Mechanism:** Direct spinal compression injures axons (Wallerian degeneration) and may impair blood supply, causing ischemia and malacia. Overall pathogenesis is still poorly understood. Appears to involve compromise of blood flow to the affected cord segment.
text.notes:
**Clinical**: Sudden flaccid paralysis and sensory deficits; extensive ascending/descending myelomalacia carries grave prognosis.

Less reported in cats due to flexible spine.

text.gross: **Cerebral **swelling and necrotizing meningoencephalitis; slide describes sparing of brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord.
text.dx: Working identification: Necrotizing meningoencephalitis (NME). Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why: Host: Young to middle-aged small-breed dogs, particularly pugs and also shih tzus, Chihuahuas and Maltese. Distinguish: NME involves cerebral cortex and meninges more than NLE, which emphasizes white matter.
text.notes:
Formerly called "Pug Encephalitis" 
The brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord are spared. 

Idiopathic immune-mediated disorder characterized by severe inflammaiton and extensive tissue destruction of the cerebral hemisphered and brain (VIN). 
Typical onset is 6months to 7 years of age. 

C/S: sudden and recurrent seizures, behavioral changes and depression, circling, stumbling, or wobbly gait (ataxia). Amaurosis, head tilt, etc. 

Can only be confirmed vis PM histopatholigical exam. 
CSF tap will show monocytic pleocytosis and elecated protein levels

text.gross: Cavitation, inflammation and glial scarring in periventricular cerebral white matter and brainstem.
text.dx: Working identification: Necrotizing leukoencephalitis (NLE). Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord / meninges. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: necrosis and cavitation (malacia) of the cerebral white matter and thalamus, accompanied by nonsuppurative inflammation
text.why:
Host: Yorkshire terriers and other small-breed dogs. Distinguish: The professor specifically says cerebral cortex and meninges are spared in NLE, unlike NME.
**Targets the deep cerebral white matter **
text.notes:
Yorkshire terrior high on list.
Age of onset is vast (1-10 years). 
Progressive neuro signs that depend on the lesion location. 
Chronic, often fatal disease

text.gross:
Dilation of ventricular system. Will look hollow on cut section. 

The portion of the ventricular system that dilates depends on the site of blockage. 
White matter is more sensitive than gray matter due to the effects of pressure from increased CSF. 

**Congenital:** *Symmetrical* enlargement and dome-shaped calvaria; the bones of the calvaria are thinned and distorted from pressure expanding the brain during gestation.
text.dx:
Brain: severe internal hydrocephalus, can be congenital or acquired. Excessive build up of CSF within the ventricular system. 
***Most common congenital CNS abnormality in domestic animals. ***
text.histo: Ependymal attenuation and pressure damage
text.why: Distinguish compressed tissue from tissue destroyed in hydranencephaly
text.notes:
Variety of causes:
 In utero viral infection (ex: feline panleukopenia)
 Developmental abnormalities in the ependyma or
ventricular system
 Infection with blockage of the ventricular system
 Genetic predisposition in some dog breeds
 Toy and brachycephalic breeds
 Compression by mass (cerebral abscesses or neoplasms)
 Cholesteatomas in the choroid plexus of the lateral
ventricles of the horse - rare
text.etiologyAgents: Congenital or acquired disturbances of CSF flow
text.speciesEvidence:
Can be very common in cats with Feline panleukopenia. 
Toy and brachycephalic breeds are affected.

text.gross: Part or complete smooth cerebrum without normal gyri and sulci. Cerebral cortext is thicker than normal on transverse section.
text.dx: Cerebrum: diffuse lissencephaly
text.histo: Abnormal neuronal migration and cortical lamination
text.why: Thought to have a genetic basis and results from an arrest or defect in neuronal migration during development since it can be a normal brain shape in birds, some laboratory rodents.
text.notes: Most commonly reported in the Lhasa apso dog.

text.gross:
****Localization is very specific to this etiology* ***
 Sharply demarcated bilateral (sometimes unilateral) sharp yellow malacic foci in globus pallidus and substantia nigra. Causes *nigropallidial encephalomalacia.*
text.dx:
Working identification: Centaurea spp. — nigropallidal encephalomalacia.
**Poisoning, chronic, and mostly in horses **
 Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Necrosis with loss of neurons.
text.why:
Horses grazing on Yellow Star Thistle or Russian knapweed. 
Chronic condition with them grazing on the plants for 1 month or longer during the hot summer, when other forage is dried and unpalatable since the thistle remains green.
text.notes: C/S: Somnolent (sleepy, drowsy), persistent chewing and difficulty in prehension of feed and drinking water.
text.etiologyAgents: Yellow Star Thistle, Russian knapweed, Centaurea ssp.

text.gross: Small cerebellum
text.dx:
Cerebellum: diffuse hypoplasia. Virus-induced. 
Virus targets the external granule layer of the cerebellum that are still dividing during the late gestational and early neonatal periods. 
Degree of hypoplasia varies depending on if the neonate or the fetus was infected.
text.histo: Granule cell depletion due to injury to proliferating cells
text.why:
The most common causes in animals are 
 Panleukopenia virus ± kitten
 Bovine viral diarrhea virus ± calves
 Classical swing fever ± pigs
text.etiologyAgents: Developmental malformation; prenatal viral injury is one possible cause, depending on species

text.gross: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) that dissects outside the central canal into the spinal cord tissue (parenchyma).
text.dx: Syringomyelia
text.histo: Absence of tissue in the spinal cord, Not lined by ependyma; typically surrounded by glial/gliotic tissue.
text.why:
Congenital and acquired forms, most commonly in calves and dog breeds. 
Proposed causes include infection, trauma, or neoplasia that result in degeneration and cavitation of the spinal cord.
text.notes:
Clinical signs in young dogs and calves with syringomyelia vary, depending on the location and size of the spinal cord lesion
 Ataxia, urinary incontinence, respiratory difficulty, muscle weakness in front and/or hind
limbs, and abnormal proprioceptive reflexes
 The syrinx can extend over several spinal cord segments
 Central canal is normal but may secondarily become compressed

text.gross:
Usually solitary, firm, well-defined, gray-white, spherical/lobulated/plaque-like and compressive, leading to pressure atrophy; hemorrhage/necrosis may alter cut surface. Soft, red, brown, or gray areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. 

**Cat:** Almost always compressive, shelled out 
**Dog: **Tend to be more attached to the underlying parenchyma and not as easy to shell out.
text.dx:
Working identification: Meningioma. 
Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Neoplastic cells
text.why:
***Most common CNS neoplasm in dogs and cats.*** Tumor arising from the meninges (arachnoid cell layer and projecting into the subdural space).
- Slow-growing
-Secondary pressure atrophy of adjacent parenchyma secondary to compression.
text.notes:
Most common CNS neoplasm in dogs and cats
 50% and 60% of intracranial neoplasms respectively
 More common in brain than spinal cord
 Dogs 7-14 years of age; Cats 10 years+

text.gross: An abnormal dilatation of the central canal of the spinal cord that leads to the formation of a cavity in which CSF may accumulate
text.dx: Hydromyelia
text.histo: Central canal absent, lined by ependymal cells (the normal lining of the central canal).
text.why:
Infectious or genetic injury that results in damage to ependymal cells lining the canal--> disruption of the normal flow of CSF--> abnormal CSF pressure gradients within the central canal.
Congenital or acquired
Acquired: **Rare** and is caused by an obstruction of the central canal CSF flow (inflammation or neoplasia)
text.notes: Clinical signs in young animals with congenital hydromyelia vary, depending on the location and size of the dilatation of the central canal in the spinal cord

text.gross:
Difficult to distinguish from adjacent parenchyma. Often displaces normal tissues. 
**Low-grade**- poorly defined mass, firm, white to pink
**High grade**- regions of hemorrhage, necrosis, cavitation
text.dx: Working identification: Astrocytoma. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Astrocyte neoplastic proliferation
text.why: Under the umbrella term of glioma. Common sites include the cerebral hemispheres and less frequently, the cerebellum and spinal cord.
text.notes: Common in Brachycephalic breeds and are the most commonly affected and generally have peak incidence from ages 5-11 years.

text.gross: Well-demarcated soft to **gelatinous** gray-to-pink-red mass with hemorrhage and possibly cystic center when large. (Gelatinous because oligodendrocytes produce myelin) larger tumors may have a central center that is cystic
text.dx: Working identification: Oligodendroglioma. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Neoplastic proliferation of oligodendrocytes.
text.why: Neoplastic oligodendrocytes. Most commonly in the dog, but far the most common glioma neoplasm (up to 70% incidence). Brachycephalic breeds have a higher occurance. Age rage is 5-11 years

text.gross: Large expansile, relatively well-circumscribed intraventricular soft gray-white to red mass; dogs tend to smooth and cats granular cut surfaces in the lecture. Aggressive tumors show invasion into the normal tissue at its margins.
text.dx: Working identification: Ependymoma. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: neoplastic ependymal cells
text.why: In the umbrella of gliomas. Neoplastic expansion of ependymal cells. Usually involves the lateral ventricle, less so the third and fourth. Can also occur in the central canal of the spinal cord. Can metastasize to the subarachnoid space due to flow of the CSF.
text.compare: Contrast choroid plexus tumor: both intraventricular, differentiation requires histology.
text.notes: Frequent in cats.

text.gross:
Expansive, well-defined granular/papillary growth within the ventricular system. 
Gray to white to red, and compresses the adjacent nervous tissues. Occurs most freqently in the fourth ventricle
text.dx: Working identification: Choroid plexus papilloma and carcinoma. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: distinguish from ependymoma
text.why: Papilloma/carcinoma of choroid plexus, commonest in dogs among species discussed; lecture notes predisposition in **Golden Retrievers** and 5–10% of canine primary brain tumors.  If it obstructs CSF flow it can produce hydrocephalus; distinguish from ependymoma via histology.

text.gross: Stenosis of the cervical vertebral canal with spinal cord compression or narrowing
text.dx: Cervical vertebral stenotic myelopathy
text.histo: Changes in the spinal cord focused on axons resulting from compression of the spinal cord
text.why:
Multifactorial pathogenesis, genetic, nutritional, growth rate.
Stenosis causes compressive trauma to the spinal cord
text.notes:
Occurs primarily in young, rapidly growing horses and large-breed dogs
**Dogs:** most common in C5-C7
**Horses:** throughout C3-C7

text.gross: Dorsal midline cranial defect (cranium bifidum) where meningeal and/or brain tissue protrude from a sac (-cele).
text.dx: Working identification: Meningoencephalocele. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why:
Hereditary in pigs and cats
Griseofulvin TX in pregnant cats during the first week of gestation
They are uncommon and sporadic in most domestic species.
text.notes:
**Meningocele-** lined by the meninges
**Meningoencephalocele**- meninges accompanied by a part of the brain

text.gross: Internal herniation of the cerebellar vermis and medulla oblongata into the foramen magnum
text.dx: Internal herniation, Chiar like malformation
text.histo: ectopic?
text.why:
Mismatch between the caudal fossa of the skull and the brain where the vault can't accommodate. 
Herniation and leads to disruption of CSF and can lead to syringomyelia
text.notes: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel is overrepresented

text.gross:
Depends on tumor type:
Hemangiosarcoma: multifocal to coalescing variably sized black lesions on the grey- white matter interface. 
Carcinomas depend, in white matter
text.dx: Working identification: Metastatic pulmonary and mammary carcinomas. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: Neoplastic growth of the originating cell in hemangiosarcoma tortuous vessels.
text.why:
Hematogenously metastasizing neoplasms will impact the brain more then the spinal cord. and CNS metastasis is more often in dogs and cats then other nonhuman species. 
**Hemangiosarcoma** is one of the most common metastasizing tumors to the brain.
text.notes: Multiple metastasizing carcinomas, mammary gland and pulmonary gland carcinomas in the dogs are reported higher than others.

text.gross: Distinctive gross lesion is **bilaterally symmetrical** yellow malacia in the ventral gray matter of spinal cord; compare with white-matter myelomalacia.
text.dx: Working identification: Selenium toxicosis in pigs. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why: Overexposure in swine feed causes neurologic deficits in feeder pigs with alertness, sternal recumbency, progression to flaccid rear-limb dysfunction and quadriplegia.
text.visualClue: Bilaterally symmetric in the ventral spinal gray matter
text.notes:
In feeder pigs with toxic selenium. Affected pgis are alert, rest in sternal recumbency. Progress to quadriplegia with flaccid paralysis of the rear limbs. 

Cutaneous manifestations are rough hair coat, partial alopecia, hoof separation, and sloughing.

text.title: Phalaris grass neurotoxicosis
text.gross: Bilaterally symmetric greenish brainstem parenchyma and gray-to-green kidney discoloration may occur.
text.dx: Working identification: Phalaris grass neurotoxicosis. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.

text.why:
Two syndromes:
1. Cardiac disorder resulting in acute death
2. Nervous system disorder characterized by ataxia, tremors, and paresis
     Accumulation of an unknown pigment within neurons of the brainstem, spinal cord, and dorsal root ganglia
    Pigment also accumulates in renal tubular epithelial cells
text.visualClue: Bilaterally symmetrical green hue to the parenchyma
text.compare: Differentiate pigment-associated Phalaris injury from hemorrhagic/malacic toxin lesions.
text.notes: Causes extensive loss of sheep and cattle; horses are also susceptible

text.title: Leukoencephalomalacia
text.gross:
Characteristic gross lesion at the time of death is malacia and liquefaction of the affected white matter
 Brainstem and cerebellum can also be impacted
 Gray matter typically spared - mechanism for this selectivity is unknown
 Edema ± marked swelling, flattening of cerebrocortical gyri
**Typically has a yellow to yellow-orange or brown-yellow color in affected tissue **
text.dx: Leukoencephalomalacia
text.histo: Liquefactive necrosis showing loss of normal architecture and eosinophilic proteinaceous debris with edema, congested blood vessels and mild hemorrhage, and gitter cells (lipid-laden macrophages) clearing the necrotic debris along with perivascular cuffing.
text.why: Consumption of moldy feed, typically Fusarium mycotoxins like fumonisin B1, moldy corn.
text.visualClue:
Yellow to brown or slightly rusted color in the white matter 
Acute
text.notes:
The most common cause is the ingestion of moldy feed with the fungus fusarium verticilliodies. Horses are the most commonly affected. 
Causes an acute, fatal neurologic disease. 

CS: Depression, somnolence, head pressing, aimless wandering, blindness or seizures. Rapid progression followed by death 1-10 days after onset.

**Polioencephalomalacia:** Gray cerebral cortex becomes yellow and soft, with autofluorescence under UV. 
Early swelling flattens gyri; later cortical separation at gray-white junction (8–10 days)
text.dx: Working identification: Thiamine deficiency — ruminant polioencephalomalacia. Specimen site: Brain / spinal cord. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.

Young aimals: prior to estabilishing ruminal flora, rumen microbs are unable to synthezise thiamine
Adults:  grain overload and overgrowth of thiaminase producing bacteria or via ingestion of thiaminase containing plants.

Ruminants, with goats less affected.

text.why:
Secondary to dietary insufficiency of Vit B1 (thiamine)
Get via ingesting of fish containing thiaminase or through thiamine-deficient diets.

text.notes:
 Clinical signs: Anorexia, vomiting, depression,
wide-based stance, ataxia, spastic paresis, circling, seizures, muscle weakness, recumbency, opisthotonus, and coma

text.title: Copper deficiency — small ruminants
text.gross:
Bilateral cerebrocortical lesions- cortex focally soft and fluctuant or collapsed, may be gelatinous softening or cavitation
Brainstem and spinal cord are affected

text.why:
***Complex and poorly understood.***
**Primary:** Copper-deficent soils or inadequate intake from forage
     Enzootic ataxia 
         Goat kid > lamb; Onset delayed up to 6 months after birth
        Brain stem and spinal cord affected
 Lordosis 
       Lambs > goat kid; Born to dams with insufficient copper levels

**Secondary:** Defective absorption from interactions with other
minerals/metals

text.dx: Working identification: Peritonitis-induced autonomic dysfunction. Specimen site: Peripheral nerve / autonomic ganglion. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo:
Central chromatolysis, edematous nerve bundles, and hyperplasia of supporting cells. May reverse if peritonitis resolves.
Look at the specific nerve or axon in the center. Significantly smaller and has a lot of clear space (edema)
text.why: GI localization. Degeneration of autonomic neurons in the myenteric and submucosal plexus in animals with peritonitis. Thought to arise from inflammatory cytokine-mediated injury to ANS neurons. May cause alterations of intestinal motility.
text.visualClue:
Affected neurons exhibit central *chromatolysis*
Nerve fiber bundles are *edematous *
text.notes:
Dysautonomia: need clinical history and supporting information. 
Degree of neuronal degeneartion may be related to the severity and type of inflammation response and the ability of those inflammatory mediators to reach the plexus.

Microphthalmia is more common and unilateral. Most often from traumatic injury to the globe via utero trauma, ischemic injury or infection

text.gross:
**Acute:**
• Auricles are red, warm and edematous
• +/- purulent material
**Chronic:**
• Thickened, bosselated, hyperpigmented epidermis
• May have stenosis of the external ear canal
• Auricular cartilage becomes less pliable

Conformation

• Breed

text.title: Acute auricular hematoma
text.gross:
**Acute: ** Auricle appears swollen, often droops. Discolored, distended by dark red, partially coagulated to coagulated fluid. 
**Chronic: ** Aurical heals by fibrosis, becomes firml thickened, and malformed.
text.mechanismSummary: Most common cause is from tramuatic head shaking secondary to otitis media or externa
text.dx: Working identification: Acute auricular hematoma. Specimen site: Auricle / ear canal / middle ear. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo:
**Acute:** Fissuring/fracture of auricular cartilage with intracartilaginous fluid accumulation, hemorrhage, and fibrin.
**Inflammation**: Variable neutrophils and macrophages; hemosiderin-laden macrophages may develop.
**Chronic**: Fibrovascular granulation tissue, collagen deposition, fibrosis, and cartilage remodeling.
text.why: Cartilage heals poorly → granulation tissue and fibrosis → scar contraction → permanent pinna thickening and deformation (cauliflower ear).
text.compare: Auricular chondritis, which features more prominent cartilage-centered inflammation.
text.notes:
**Instructor L78 · slides 10**
**Etiology / pathogenesis:** Head shaking from otitis externa/media tears blood vessels; dogs, pigs and cats emphasized.
**Gross, histology and clinical differentiation:** Swollen often drooping pinna distended by dark-red partially clotted blood.
**🔎 Master chart · visual recognition:** Fluctuant swollen pinna distended with dark red blood following head shaking.
**↔ Master chart · distinguish from:** A blood pocket differs from a discrete neoplastic solid mass.

text.title: Auricular chondritis
text.gross: Bilateral auricles are swollen, erythematous, painful, pruritic, and variably alopecic and curled.
text.mechanismSummary: Cartilage-associated immune/inflammatory injury → chondrocyte damage and fibrosis → distorted pinna.
text.dx: Working identification: Auricular chondritis. Specimen site: Auricle / ear canal / middle ear. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo:
Auricular cartilage is distorted with transformation of the normally basophilic cartilaginous matrix to an eosinophilic matrix
• Infiltration of the ear and cartilage by mixed lymphoplasmacytic to granulomatous inflammation
text.why: Etiology / pathogenesis: Usually cats <3 years; bilateral painful pruritic red, swollen, curled, sometimes alopecic pinnae. Gross, histology and clinical differentiation: Histology: cartilage matrix shifts from basophilic to eosinophilic, with lymphoplasmacytic-to-granulomatous infiltrates.
text.visualClue: Bilaterally swollen auricles with curled ears. Cats less than 3 years of age.

text.mechanismSummary: Proliferates in moist areas where the skin barrier is compromised.

text.title: Fetal mummification
text.gross: Retained fetus is dry, flattened or shriveled, leathery brown-black and largely retains recognizable form; usually no foul-smelling purulent fluid. May coexist with live littermates in pigs.
text.mechanismSummary: Fetal death after skin formation → sterile uterine retention → fluid resorption → desiccation and mummification
text.dx: Uterus: fetal mummification, with retained desiccated fetal remains.
text.histo: Gross pattern is usually more diagnostic than histology; autolysis and dehydration occur without bacterial suppuration.
text.why: Fetus dies after skin develops while cervix remains closed and uterine contents stay sterile; fetal fluids are resorbed and membranes contract around preserved tissue. No bacterial infection.
text.visualClue: Dry leathery recognizable fetus with little or no putrid exudate. NO bacterial infection.
text.compare: Maceration involves bacterial infection with fragmented soft tissues, bone remnants and pus; emphysematous fetus has gas and putrefaction.
text.notes:
**L77 · EXAM HIGHLIGHT (Fetus retained, no bacterial decomposition; mare twin and sow examples)** Most commonly seen in multiparous species.
**SPECIES + GROSS:** Swine is the most common, cattle and occasionally mare twin; preserved, dry brown-black leathery fetal outline and little/no purulence.
**WHY / PATHOGENESIS:** Sterile retained fetal death after skin differentiation → resorption of fluids → dehydration and retained preserved form.

**Essential condition**: Fetal death with NO bacterial infection, retained fetus and sufficiently mature fetal skin; retained CL may maintain gestation.
**Gross**: Dehydrated brown/black leathery fetus, sticky mucus, intact recognizable form; lack of foul odor/pus.
**Species**: Especially sow and one twin in mare; large mummified bovine fetus may take months to fully desiccate.
**Comparison**: Mummification preserves shape; maceration destroys soft tissue due to infection.

text.title: Fetal maceration
text.gross: Disintegrating fetal tissue/bones with purulent exudate, severe endometritis or pyometra; less preserved than mummy.
text.mechanismSummary: Fetal death plus bacterial invasion → autolysis/putrefaction → soft tissue breakdown and suppurative endometritis.
text.dx: Working identification: Fetal maceration. Specimen site: Placenta / fetus / uterus. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why: Microbial decay aggravates dam's uterine pathology. ↔ Master chart · distinguish from: Presence of pus/debris separates from sterile dry mummification.
text.visualClue: Infected uterine contents with disintegrated fetal soft tissue, bones and often purulent foul exudate. Retained fetal bones amid purulent liquefied tissue, indicating bacterial contamination.
text.compare: **important term**Mummy maintains recognizable dehydrated shape without pus; emphysematous fetus is distended by gas.
text.notes:
Requires the presence of an infection in the uterus. 
If the early embryo succumbs to uterine or embryonic infection, maceration is usually followed by resorption within the uterus or expulsion along with a small amount of purulent exudate ex. Pyometra, Acutre endometritis. 

The presence of bacteria basically causes destruction of fetal tissue, making the infection worse.

text.title: Emphysematous fetus
text.gross: Fetus grossly swollen, distended with foul gas, crepitant on palpation; can deflate with incision.
text.mechanismSummary: Gas-forming bacterial invasion → fetal putrefaction → tissue gas → dam risks toxemia, metritis and dystocia.
text.dx: Working identification: Emphysematous fetus. Specimen site: Placenta / fetus / uterus. Formulate the final morphologic diagnosis from the visible tissue, distribution, severity and process; etiology requires supporting evidence.
text.histo: No distinctive histologic pattern is specified in this lecture section. Do not infer an organism or cell type from gross morphology alone.
text.why: Distended crepitant fetuses with putrid gas after prolonged obstetric complication or open cervix.
text.visualClue: Distended crepitant fetuses with putrid gas after prolonged obstetric complication or open cervix.
text.compare: Mummy is dry sterile and shrunken; maceration produces soft tissue dissolution and loose bones.
text.notes:
**Requirement**: Putrefactive GAS-PRODUCING bacterial invasion through patent cervix, often dystocia or incomplete abortion.
**Course**: May lead to maceration and foul suppurative metritis, with thick uterine wall and severe maternal disease.

specimen-custom-68-cerebrospinal-nematod.title: Cerebrospinal Nematodiasis
specimen-custom-68-cerebrospinal-nematod.gross:
Linear tracts of necrosis and hemorrhage
Migration results in endothelial injury, vasculitis and thrombosis. May cause vascular occlusion and infarction.
specimen-custom-68-cerebrospinal-nematod.histo: If larvae are in sections, they can induce a mononuclear cell inflammatory exudate, often including eosinophiles
specimen-custom-68-cerebrospinal-nematod.why: Aberrant migration of larval nematodes within the CNS

specimen-custom-69-syringomyelia.title: Syringomyelia
specimen-custom-69-syringomyelia.gross: Cavity (syrinx) that forms in the spinal cord.
specimen-custom-69-syringomyelia.histo: Absence of tissue in the spinal cord
specimen-custom-69-syringomyelia.why:
Congenital and acquired forms, most commonly in calves and dog breeds. 
Proposed causes include infection, trauma, or neoplasia that result in degeneration and cavitation of the spinal cord.

specimen-custom-69-hydromyelia.title: Hydromyelia
specimen-custom-69-hydromyelia.gross: An abnormal dilatation of the central canal of the spinal cord that leads to the formation of a cavity in which CSF may accumulate
specimen-custom-69-hydromyelia.why:
Infectious or genetic injury that results in damage to ependymal cells lining the canal--> disruption of the normal flow of CSF--> abnormal CSF pressure gradients within the central canal.
Congenital or acquired
Acquired: **Rare** and is caused by an obstruction of the central canal CSF flow (inflammation or neoplasia)

specimen-custom-69-cervical-vertebral-st.title: Cervical vertebral stenotic myelopathy (Wobbler syndrome)
specimen-custom-69-cervical-vertebral-st.gross: Stenosis of the cervical vertebral canal with spinal cord compression or narrowing
specimen-custom-69-cervical-vertebral-st.histo: Changes in the spinal cord focused on axons resutling from compression of the spinal cord
specimen-custom-69-cervical-vertebral-st.why: Multifactorial pathogenesis, genetic, nutritional, growth rate

specimen-custom-69-chiari-like-malformat.title: Chiari-Like Malformation
specimen-custom-69-chiari-like-malformat.gross: Internal herniation of the cerebellar vermis and medulla oblongata into the foramen magnum
specimen-custom-69-chiari-like-malformat.why:
Mismatch between the caudal fossa of the skull and the brain where the vault can't accommodate. 
Herniation and leads to disruption of CSF and can lead to syringomyelia

specimen-custom-69-leukoencephalomalacia.title: Leukoencephalomalacia
specimen-custom-69-leukoencephalomalacia.gross:
Characteristic gross lesion at the time of death is malacia and liquefaction of the affected white matter
 Brainstem and cerebellum can also be impacted
 Gray matter typically spared - mechanism for this selectivity is unknown
 Edema ± marked swelling, flattening of cerebrocortical gyri
**Typically has a yellow to yellow-orange or brown-yellow color in affected tissue **
specimen-custom-69-leukoencephalomalacia.histo: Liquefactive necrosis showing loss of normal architecture and eosinophilic proteinaceous debris with edema, congested blood vessels and mild hemorrhage, and gitter cells (lipid-laden macrophages) clearing the necrotic debris along with perivascular cuffing.
specimen-custom-69-leukoencephalomalacia.why: Consumption of moldy feed, typically Fusarium mycotoxins like fumonisin B1, moldy corn.

specimen-custom-78-anophthalmia-and-micr.title: Anophthalmia and Microphthalmia
specimen-custom-78-anophthalmia-and-micr.gross:
**Anophthalmia**: Complete absence of the eye, mostly bilateral
**Microphthalmia:** Small, disorganized globe in an orbit of a normally sized eye, unilateral
specimen-custom-78-anophthalmia-and-micr.why:
Failure to develop the eye or a small amount in a normal orbit. 
Microphthalmia is more common and unilateral. Most often from traumatic injury to the globe via utero trauma, ischemic injury or infection
